messages: REFUSED as a bound. There is no measured economic or operational lifetime for a physical server in any primary source the research could reach. The "4-5 years" figure is ubiquitous and untraceable and is graded folklore. US-GAAP useful-life guidance for data-processing equipment is a tax convention, not an operational life. Asserting it would put a number in the spec that nothing supports, and D13's own argument — data that reads as fake undermines every question asked of it — cuts both ways: so does data built on a figure nobody measured. The ubiquitous version is the ubiquitous 'servers last four to five years', attributed to no primary measurement; where folklore is the only source, the catalogue declines to assert it, and a distributional check is used instead.

REFUSED as a bound. Same as compute_node: no measured operational lifetime exists. Vendors publish support end-of-life dates, which bound the SUPPORT life of a product model and not the economic life of the thing in the rack. The ubiquitous version is the ubiquitous 'network kit lasts five years', with no primary measurement behind it; where folklore is the only source, the catalogue declines to assert it, and a distributional check is used instead.

REFUSED as a bound. VMware/Broadcom's own performance engineering (June 2025) says the opposite of a bound: "The rapidly increasing churn rate of customer environments ... So if we can't predict what will be virtualized, what its requirements are, or HOW LONG ITS LIFECYCLE WILL BE, we can't create a static ratio." A hard bound on VM lifetime is therefore not merely unsourced, it is contradicted by the vendor. What IS supportable is a DISTRIBUTIONAL check — see plausibility.creation_rate_consistent — and that is what this catalogue asserts instead. The ubiquitous version is any fixed VM lifetime, including the 18-month figure the vendor's own guidance declines to give; where folklore is the only source, the catalogue declines to assert it, and a distributional check is used instead.

REFUSED as a bound. No measured distribution of firewall-rule lifetime exists in any source reached. What is measured is the ACCUMULATION (69% unused, and the cycle nobody can break: more unused access, more complexity, slower cleanup, more unused access), which is a rate and not a lifetime. A lifetime here would be a guess wearing a unit. The ubiquitous version is any fixed firewall-rule review cycle; where folklore is the only source, the catalogue declines to assert it, and a distributional check is used instead.

REFUSED as a bound. Every figure found traces to vendor content marketing with no disclosed method, and the research declined to put a number in the spec. The THRESHOLD (45 days, CIS 5.3) is authoritative and is asserted as a parameter; the RATE is not available and is not asserted. Asserting a rate would also be the fig-leaf disease D30 exists to prevent: a proportion with no channel behind it is a restatement. The ubiquitous version is the ubiquitous '15-30% of accounts are dormant', graded folklore with no disclosed method; where folklore is the only source, the catalogue declines to assert it, and a distributional check is used instead.
grouped.title: The bounds this catalogue REFUSES to assert — a rule whose normal behaviour is to FIRE
